_readme: The machine-readable answer to 'is this the official IdleToken build, and where
did it legitimately come from?' (threat register DIST-01..DIST-07, DIST-11..14,
This file is data on purpose. An About box that prints the same facts proves
nothing — a fork can print anything. What is useful is a published record that
a user, a mirror operator or a journalist can fetch from the official origin
over a channel we do not control the copy of, and compare against the bytes
they actually downloaded. scripts/verify_release.sh does exactly that
comparison, and it needs no IdleToken installation to run.
Everything here is either public by nature (a repository URL, a public key) or
a statement we want copied widely. Nothing here is a secret, and nothing here

trademarkPolicy: The source is Apache-2.0. A licence to use the code is not a licence to use
the name. Forks and redistributions must not present themselves as IdleToken
or as an official build: change the product name, the bundle identifier, the
icon and the updater key before publishing (DIST-01, DIST-14).
A fork that keeps the name while changing privacy, billing or model behaviour
is the specific case this asks people not to create — users cannot tell, and
the resulting incident lands on the official project.

_note: Downloads from anywhere else are not official builds, whatever they are named.
This includes software-download portals, cloud-drive links, chat-group
attachments and 'green' or 'cracked' repacks (DIST-02, DIST-03).
We do not buy search advertising, so a sponsored result for 'IdleToken
download' is not us.

_minimumSupportedVersionNote: DIST-07. An old build with a known flaw is dangerous in two ways, and the
second is the one that needs a published field: a malicious fork can simply
delete the update check, or show a fake 'you are up to date'. Nothing the
client does about its own version can be trusted.
This field is therefore for the SERVER, not the client. The platform reads
it and decides what to do with a session claiming an older version — warn,
restrict, or refuse. Raise it when a release fixes something that makes
older builds unsafe to keep serving, and say so in the release notes.
Note the honest limit: the version a request claims is self-reported and
copyable, so this floor stops honest-but-stale clients, not attackers. It is
a patch-adoption lever, not an authentication mechanism.

_note: An installed official client accepts an update only if its signature verifies
against this key. The key id is short enough to read out over the phone and is
the value to compare when someone claims to be shipping an IdleToken update.
This protects the update path of an already-official install. It says nothing
about a first install — an attacker's build simply carries the attacker's own
key and updates itself happily (DIST-05). That is what the artifact digests
below are for.

windows.expectedUserExperience: SmartScreen shows a blue 'Windows protected your PC' box for the official installer.
_note: Stated plainly because the alternative is worse: if we implied the official
installer is signed, a user who sees the blue box would conclude their
download is fake, and a user trained to expect the box clicks through the
attacker's box too (DIST-04). Until a certificate exists, the SHA-256
comparison below is the check that actually distinguishes the two.

macos.expectedUserExperience: Gatekeeper refuses the first launch; the app must be opened from the context menu.

steps: 1. Download the installer AND the provenance json + .sig from the official release page.
3. It refuses unless the provenance signature verifies against key 28F23C3CE24BFDE9 and the installer's SHA-256 is listed in it.
The verifier is pure Python plus shasum. It does not need IdleToken installed, so it works before a first install — the moment the update signature cannot help.

officialTools: The diagnostics bundle produced by the client's own Settings screen
weWillNeverAskYouTo: run a 'repair tool', 'accelerator pack', 'driver fixer' or 'updater' downloaded from a link
send an updater private key, a platform JWT, an API key, a pairing code or a cluster PSK
disable the signature check or install an update from outside the app
paste a command into a terminal to 'fix' a support case
_note: DIST-11. A support process with no published shape is one an impersonator can
invent. The diagnostics bundle is the only artifact support ever asks for, and
it is built by the client from an allowlist so it cannot carry tokens or
prompts.
DIST-12. There is no official mobile app and no official browser front end at
this time. Anything presenting itself as one is not ours — which is a much
easier claim for a user to check than judging a convincing screenshot.
When one ships, it gets its own entry here with its store identifiers, and the
pairing authorisation boundary is stated with it.

notAnAuthenticator: Nothing in this file authenticates a running client to the platform. Version
strings, user agents and build stamps are copyable by anyone who reads the
source (threat register §1.1), so the platform must apply the same server-side
rules to every request regardless of what the client claims to be. This file
answers a different question: 'are these BYTES the ones the project published?'
